extracted.intended_audience: journalists, Reuters reporters, editors and copy-editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rules for word usage, punctuation, capitalization, names, and other stylistic choices for news copy produced by Reuters and its journalists worldwide.

rubrics_metrics.name: between, among
rubrics_metrics.description: Between is restricted to two choices or two parties. Among is for several options or parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use between for bilateral contacts (e.g. relations between France and Germany). Use among for a collective linkage (e.g. relations among the NATO states). If there are just two groups to choose from, use between even if it looks like several (example contrast provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: biannual, biennial
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No hyphen. Prefer twice-yearly instead of biannual, and every two years rather than biennial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bible, bible
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upper case when referring to the book itself; lower case when used as a metaphor.

rubrics_metrics.name: biblical
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not 'Biblical' (i.e., do not capitalise).

rubrics_metrics.name: bid, in a bid to
rubrics_metrics.description: 'in a bid to' is sloppy and verbose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can usually be removed by rewriting, or replaced with an active verb such as 'tried to' or 'attempted'.

rubrics_metrics.name: bight, bite
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bight is a wide bay or a coil. You bite with your teeth.

rubrics_metrics.name: billion
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric and stylistic conventions for 'billion' in Reuters copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Reuters services billion means one thousand million. Spell the word out (but 'bln' okay in headlines). Always use figures before million and billion (e.g. 2 billion). For ranges use '1.2 billion to 1.4 billion' not '1.2-1.4 billion'. See also figures, trillion.

rubrics_metrics.name: bimonthly, semimonthly
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid these words. Write 'every other month' for bimonthly and 'twice a month' for semimonthly.

rubrics_metrics.name: bin Laden
rubrics_metrics.description: How to refer to Osama bin Laden in Reuters copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Osama bin Laden'. Use 'bin Laden' at second reference. If relevant mention he is Saudi-born (note about stripped Saudi citizenship).

rubrics_metrics.name: bird
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bird is an animal; therefore write 'birds and mammals' or 'birds and reptiles', not 'birds and animals'.

rubrics_metrics.name: birdie, birdies
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One stroke under par in golf.

rubrics_metrics.name: BIS
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bank for International Settlements; international organisation fostering monetary and financial co-operation and serving as a bank for central banks. The Basel Committee of the BIS sets standards and guidelines. See www.bis.org

rubrics_metrics.name: biweekly
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can mean twice a week or once every two weeks. Avoid using it.

rubrics_metrics.name: black
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage guidance when referring to race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fine as an adjective (e.g. 'Obama will be the first black U.S. president'). As a noun, the plural is acceptable where it might contrast with another group (e.g. 'doctors found differences between the treatment offered to whites and blacks'). Do not use 'black' as a singular noun; avoid constructions like 'the first black to become U.S. president'—prefer 'the first black U.S. president'. See section on race.

rubrics_metrics.name: black box
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular term for aircraft recording equipment. Although not actually black, the term may be used if it is made clear the reference is to a plane's flight recorder or flight-deck voice recorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: blame
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution about apportioning blame in reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat with caution; in accidents apportioning blame can cause legal problems. Strong sourcing is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: blast off, blastoff
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One word for the noun (blastoff) and two words for the verb (blast off).

rubrics_metrics.name: blazon, blaze
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You 'blazon' (ostentatiously display) your wealth, and 'blaze' a trail.

rubrics_metrics.name: blind
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe people as 'blind' only if they are totally without sight. Otherwise write that their 'sight is impaired' or that they have 'partial vision'.

rubrics_metrics.name: blitzkrieg
rubrics_metrics.guidance: German for lightning war or violent attack. Use the short form 'blitz' only for heavy air attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: bloc, block
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'bloc' is a combination of units, parties or nations. A 'block' is a lump.

rubrics_metrics.name: blockbuster
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sparingly unless you have figures to support profit or return on investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: blond, blonde
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'blond' for a man, 'blonde' for a woman. The adjective is always 'blond'.

rubrics_metrics.name: blue blood / blue-blooded
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'blue blood' is a noun; 'blue-blooded' is the adjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: blueprint
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tired cliché; use 'plan' or 'proposal' instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: B’nai B’rith
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note apostrophes in the name.

rubrics_metrics.name: bogey, bogie, bogy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bogey is a golf term (one stroke above par). A 'bogie' is a trolley. A 'bogy' is a bugbear or object of dread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bombay
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Mumbai' unless it is a proper name (e.g. The Bombay Stock Exchange). Similarly use Chennai (not Madras) and Kolkata (not Calcutta).

rubrics_metrics.name: bona fide
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'bona fide'.

rubrics_metrics.name: bond
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bond is a legal contract where a borrower issues a certificate promising specific interest for a fixed duration and redemption at maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: bondholder
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One word: 'bondholder'.

rubrics_metrics.name: book titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalisation rules for titles of works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books, films, plays, poems, operas, songs and works of art: capitalise every word in the title apart from conjunctions, articles, particles and short prepositions (examples provided). Same rule for radio and TV programmes other than news and current affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: bored with
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'bored with' not 'bored of'.

rubrics_metrics.name: born, borne
rubrics_metrics.description: Use cases for born vs borne.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'He was born on Tuesday' (passive). 'She has borne 10 children' (active) and 'borne the burden of...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bosporus
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Bosporus', not 'Bosphorus'.

rubrics_metrics.name: both
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Both sides agreed' is tautological; avoid constructions like 'They both went to the same play'—write 'They went to the same play.'

rubrics_metrics.name: boss
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid in serious contexts because of pejorative/slang connotations; acceptable informally and in sports. Use 'manager' or 'coach' in formal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Botswana
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Its people are 'Batswana' (singular and plural).

rubrics_metrics.name: boy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any male over 18 is a 'man'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boy Scouts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Now just 'Scouts'.

rubrics_metrics.name: boycott, embargo
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'boycott' is the refusal of a group to deal with a person or use a commodity. An 'embargo' is a legal ban on trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: brackets
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an entire sentence is in brackets, put the full stop inside. If a sentence has a bracketed section at the end, the full stop goes outside. If a bracketed section in the middle is followed by a comma, the comma goes outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Braille
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Braille' is capitalised.

rubrics_metrics.name: brand names
rubrics_metrics.description: When to use brand names and how to format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a generic equivalent unless the brand is important. When used, follow the owner's capitalisation (e.g. Aspro not aspro) and observe legal protection. Avoid exclamation points, and follow company preferences (e.g. eBay becomes Ebay at sentence start).

rubrics_metrics.name: breach, breech
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Breach' is a break; 'breech' is the lower part (e.g., breech birth).

rubrics_metrics.name: break in
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'break in' is the verb; 'break-in' is the noun.

rubrics_metrics.name: break point
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two words in tennis scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brent
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Brent blend' is a benchmark crude oil from the British North Sea used for pricing other crude oils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Britain vs England/UK
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'England' as a synonym for Britain or the United Kingdom. Britain comprises England, Scotland and Wales. The United Kingdom comprises Britain and Northern Ireland. Use 'Britain' unless the Irish context is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: British Isles
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A geographical, not political term; comprises the UK, islands under the British Crown (Channel Islands, Isle of Man) and the Republic of Ireland.

rubrics_metrics.name: British spelling vs American
rubrics_metrics.description: Spelling conventions by origin of copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy originating in the Americas should follow North American spelling (color, defense, aging, etc.). Copy from elsewhere should follow British spelling. Always stick to official spellings for American names/titles (e.g. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates). In American sports coverage use American terms and spellings (center, maneuver, defense, postseason, etc.). Watch regional words that might be hard to translate.

rubrics_metrics.name: broach, brooch
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Broach' means to pierce or open up. 'Brooch' is an ornamental clasp.

rubrics_metrics.name: broken quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: When to use partial/broken quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use broken quotes if the words quoted are not contentious (e.g. He said she was a great soldier). Use broken quotes if the language is inflammatory or colourful (e.g. She said he was a 'stinking, rotten coward').

rubrics_metrics.name: brownout
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary voltage reduction to conserve electric power; contrasted with blackout (shut down).

rubrics_metrics.name: BSE
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bovine spongiform encephalopathy, or mad cow disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: burgeoning
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An overused adjective. 'Burgeoning' means beginning to grow rapidly; otherwise use 'growing'.

rubrics_metrics.name: burglary
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal definitions vary but usually involve entering a building unlawfully to commit a crime — be aware of local legal differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burma / Myanmar
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Myanmar'. In copy refer to 'Myanmar, formerly known as Burma.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Burmese names
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite rule about dropping honorifics, keep the full name at second reference. 'U' means Mr and 'Daw' means Mrs. When 'U' is followed by a single name it should be retained (e.g., U Nu).

rubrics_metrics.name: burqa
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not 'burka'. A one-piece head-to-toe covering with a headband and a cloth mesh to cover the face but allow vision. Most frequent in Afghanistan and Pakistan. Some languages use 'burqa' for other coverings — avoid that usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: but
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid in leads and sentence starts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid where possible, particularly in leads. It is imprecise and can imply bias if placed between differing versions of events (use a full stop and a new sentence instead). Do not start a sentence with 'but'.

rubrics_metrics.name: by (prefix hyphenation)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a prefix 'by' needs no hyphen, except in 'by-election', 'by-law', 'by-product'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byelorussia
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Belarus'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byzantine
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalise 'Byzantine'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cabinet
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalise when referring to a grouping of senior government ministers, heads of department or presidential advisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalisation (general rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad rules for when to capitalise words in news copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put first letters in capitals to make terms limited and specific. Abbreviations follow the capitalisation of the unabbreviated form. Capitalise academic/aristocratic/corporate/official/military/religious titles when they immediately precede a personal name; lowercase otherwise (examples provided). Acronyms: capitalise each letter if formed from capitalised initial letters (e.g. NATO); if formed from syllables, capitalise only first letter. Avoid acronyms where possible. Specific rules/examples are given for armed forces, astronomical bodies (capitalise named bodies but not 'sun', 'moon', 'earth' except in special cases), drugs (capitalise synthetic drug names like Ecstasy), geographical/geological names (capitalise proper names, exceptions for particles and compass refs), geopolitical adjectives (capitalise 'Western' etc.), government ministers (capitalise when preceding name), government bodies (capitalise integral part of full name), hyphenated titles (capitalise both parts), legislative bodies (capitalise official names, but lower case in plurals), nationality and race (capitalise words denoting nationality, race or language), nicknames (treat as proper names), occupations (do not capitalise generic occupational descriptors), politics (capitalise party names but lower case generic references), proper names and proper nouns (rules and exceptions), publications (no quotation marks around masthead; don't capitalise articles/particles in mastheads), books/films/works (capitalise words except small conjunctions/articles), quotes after colons (capitalise first word).

rubrics_metrics.name: carat, caret
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Carat' measures weight in precious stones and purity in gold. 'Caret' is a proofreader's mark to show insertion. In American style 'karat' measures gold purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: carry out
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A weak synonym for 'do'; use a stronger verb to describe the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: casino
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plural: casinos.

rubrics_metrics.name: caution (verb)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a verb prefer 'warn'. Do not write 'He cautioned that war was imminent' (use 'warned').

rubrics_metrics.name: CD-ROM
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'CD-ROM'.

rubrics_metrics.name: ceasefire
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'ceasefire' is one word as a noun. The verb is 'to cease fire'.

rubrics_metrics.name: celebrant, celebrator
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'celebrant' takes part in a religious ceremony; a 'celebrator' takes part in a revel.

rubrics_metrics.name: celibacy, chastity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Celibacy' is unmarried (often by vow); 'chastity' is sexual purity or virginity. One can be chaste but not celibate, and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: cellphone
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One word: 'cellphone'.

rubrics_metrics.name: cement, concrete
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cement is one constituent of concrete. Use 'concrete block', not 'cement block'.

rubrics_metrics.name: centuries
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out numbers one to nine for centuries (ninth century); write 10 and above in figures (20th century). No capital letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: CEO
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'chief executive officer' on first reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: chairman, chairwoman
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'chairman' or 'chairwoman' (not 'chair' or 'chairperson').

rubrics_metrics.name: catch-22
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalised and hyphenated; means an absurd no‑win situation. Use sparingly as it's a cliché.

rubrics_metrics.name: cave in, cave-in
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two words for the verb ('cave in'); one word for the noun ('cave-in').

rubrics_metrics.name: caution vs warn
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'warn' as a verb; avoid 'caution' in formulations like 'He cautioned that...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: company names
rubrics_metrics.description: How to present company names in copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the full legal company name (including Inc, Ltd, Plc etc.) at first reference. If clumsy, full legal name can be given at second reference. Give the name in its original language if in Latin characters unless the company prefers an English name. Observe spelling, capitalisation and punctuation used by the company; do not use a point after abbreviations (Inc not Inc.). Use standard abbreviations for company type. Do not pluralise company names (use 'Ford', not 'Fords'). Use singular verbs for companies. Eliminate exclamation points from company names (e.g. Yahoo!, Yum! should be presented without exclamation). Keep lower case in company names except at the start of a sentence (e.g. eBay becomes Ebay).
